flagged_chunks.source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
flagged_chunks.text: Under the NIAID addendum, a peanut skin-prick wheal of 0-2mm supports home introduction; 3-7mm supports an in-office supervised feeding or graded challenge; 8mm or larger is treated as probable allergy, and the infant should be managed as allergic, though in-office introduction can still be considered if the family and provider agree.

flagged_chunks.source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
flagged_chunks.text: The STAR trial gave raw pasteurized egg powder from 4 months to eczema-affected infants but was stopped prematurely: about a third of the 4-month-old participants were already both egg-sensitized and reactive to egg at trial entry, suggesting some infants were sensitized before the trial even started. The trend favored egg introduction (33% vs 51% egg allergy at 12 months) but did not reach statistical significance.

flagged_chunks.source_name: Greenhawt & Fleischer — Primary Prevention of Food Allergy (Curr Allergy Asthma Rep 2017)
flagged_chunks.text: The German HEAP trial found no significant reduction in egg sensitization or allergy with thrice-weekly raw pasteurized egg from 4-6 months, and three of twelve already egg-sensitized infants in the intervention arm had severe reactions on first exposure — evidence against introducing egg this way without prior screening in that population.

flagged_chunks.source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
flagged_chunks.guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
flagged_chunks.text: For infants with severe eczema (high risk), APAPARI recommends beginning clinical evaluation (history, skin-prick and/or specific IgE testing, focused on egg and peanut where peanut prevalence is high) from 4 months of age but ideally not later than 10 months, in countries with ready access to allergy expertise, followed by supervised oral food challenge if sensitized.

flagged_chunks.source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
flagged_chunks.guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
flagged_chunks.text: In countries with limited access to allergy expertise, APAPARI recommends that families who want early introduction for a severely eczematous infant have careful oral food challenges performed in the office of a doctor trained in recognizing and managing allergic reactions, rather than skipping supervision altogether.

flagged_chunks.source_name: Tham et al. — APAPARI Consensus: Early Allergenic Food Introduction, Asian Perspective (Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2018)
flagged_chunks.guidance_status: current (APAPARI regional adaptation of Western guidance)
flagged_chunks.text: If an infant is sensitized and does not pass a supervised oral food challenge, that specific food is avoided in the regular diet for the time being, and the family is guided to re-evaluate later with their allergy provider rather than treating the result as a permanent restriction.

flagged_chunks.source_name: Shakhova et al. — Evolution of Approaches to Primary Prevention of Food Allergy: Elimination to Early Introduction (Current Pediatrics 2025)
flagged_chunks.text: Evidence on cow's milk formula timing is mixed: a Japanese study (Sakihara et al. 2021) found adding a small amount of cow's-milk-based formula around 2 months of age significantly reduced later cow's milk allergy in breastfed infants, whereas the ABS trial (Urashima et al. 2019) found introducing unmodified cow's-milk-protein formula within the first 3 days of life increased the risk of cow's milk allergy compared with an amino-acid formula — suggesting a possible 'window of tolerance' that opens somewhat later than the immediate newborn period.

flagged_chunks.source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
flagged_chunks.text: All EAACI recommendations in this guideline apply to infants up to 1 year and young children up to 5 years, regardless of their baseline risk of allergy, and are intended for infants who have not yet developed a food allergy; children with symptoms suggestive of existing food allergy should be referred to a specialist allergy service rather than managed under these prevention recommendations.

flagged_chunks.source_name: Halken et al. — EAACI Guideline: Preventing the Development of Food Allergy in Infants and Young Children (2020 update, Pediatr Allergy Immunol 2021)
flagged_chunks.text: This guideline does not include a specific recommendation or corrected-age adjustment for premature infants; its recommendations are stated generally for infants up to 1 year and young children up to 5 years, without a stated premature-infant subgroup analysis.

flagged_chunks.source_name: NIAID Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy in the United States
flagged_chunks.text: Mild allergic reaction symptoms include a new rash or a few hives around the mouth/face; more severe symptoms include lip/face/tongue swelling, vomiting, widespread hives, difficulty breathing, wheeze, repetitive coughing, change in skin color, or sudden lethargy - any of which warrant immediate medical attention.
